title: Body and training
description: See how practice, food and recovery shape training.
author: claude

topic.title: Body and training
topic.description: Short cases from hostel rooms, gyms and hot days.

modules.title: Train, recover and read the clues

concepts.title: Progressive overload
concepts.hook: Ten clean push-ups may feel hard at first and easier after weeks of practice. What changed?
concepts.rule: Muscles adapt to repeated resistance work. For more long-term progress, the work can grow in a measured way, such as more clean reps or a harder load.

claims.text: Resistance work can build strength; a rising challenge can support further progress over time.

items.stem: In a hostel room, ten clean push-ups feel easier after a few weeks. Which change can add a fresh challenge?

options.text: Try one more clean rep.
options.feedback: A small rise in good work can give the muscles a new task after they adapt.

options.text: Add weight at once, even if the last reps lose form.
options.feedback: More load may look like progress. A clean rep can add a safer new task.

options.text: Switch to a brand new move every visit.
options.feedback: Changing moves all the time makes progress hard to track. A small, steady rise on one move gives a clear new task.

items.stem: At a college gym, Asha adds a small load once her usual reps feel smooth. What idea is she using?

options.text: A measured rise in resistance.
options.feedback: The work gets a little harder as her ability grows, which is the overload idea.

options.text: Proof that only load, not reps, can track progress.
options.feedback: The added load is easy to see. More clean reps can also raise the work.

options.text: Proof that muscles stop changing after a month.
options.feedback: Muscles keep adapting when the work rises bit by bit. Her small added load shows that steady rise.

items.stem: For progressive overload, a trainee compares two plans: add one clean push-up or add weight that makes form rough. About how many plans make a measured rise in work?

options.text: One plan: add the clean rep.
options.feedback: One more controlled rep raises the work a little. The rough load jump is not measured progress.

options.text: Both plans raise the challenge well.
options.feedback: A large weight jump with rough form is not the measured rise the rule describes.

options.text: Zero plans; only heavier weight counts.
options.feedback: More good reps can raise the work even when the load stays the same.

items.stem: What can make a familiar lift a little harder over time?

options.text: More clean reps with the same load.
options.feedback: Doing a little more sound work is one way to raise the task.

options.text: Add weight before the current lift feels controlled.
options.feedback: More weight can look like progress. First get the move right, then add a small load.

options.text: The same reps and load each week for a year.
options.feedback: Repeating the same task keeps it familiar. Without a small rise, the work stops being a fresh challenge.

items.stem: A trainee keeps the same easy set for months and expects that set to keep giving the same new strength gains. What is missing?

options.text: The body can adapt to that task.
options.feedback: Once work feels easier, a measured rise can offer a new reason to adapt.

options.text: A set that was once hard keeps driving the same new gains.
options.feedback: That set once gave a useful task. As it gets easy, a small rise can help again.

options.text: Only a heavier weight could renew the challenge.
options.feedback: More weight is one route, which makes it tempting. More clean reps can raise the task too.

items.stem: Fill the gap: practice, adapt, then add a small new ___.

options.text: Challenge.
options.feedback: A fresh task can keep resistance work useful as the old task gets easier.

options.text: Weight increase at every session.
options.feedback: Adding weight is one way to progress, but a clean rep or another gradual change can also raise the challenge.

options.text: Rest day.
options.feedback: Rest matters, but the step after adapting is a slightly harder task. That fresh challenge drives more change.

items.stem: A friend says overload means a heavier weight at every session, even when reps get rough. What needs fixing?

options.text: Progress can come from more good reps too.
options.feedback: The challenge can rise in more than one way; a forced load jump is not required.

options.text: Only added weight can count as overload.
options.feedback: Adding weight is easy to track, but more good reps can also raise the work.

options.text: The weight must rise even when form breaks down.
options.feedback: A heavier bar can feel like progress. A sound move matters more than a forced jump.

items.stem: Put the steps of a gradual training rise in order.

options.text: Pick a move you can do with clean form.
options.feedback: A sound start gives a task the body can repeat safely and learn from.

options.text: Repeat it until the clean reps feel easier.
options.feedback: Practice gives the body time to adapt before the task is raised.

options.text: Add one small new challenge, like one more rep.
options.feedback: Once the old task feels easier, a small rise gives the muscles a fresh job.

misconceptions.name: More weight every visit
misconceptions.correction: A gradual rise can use clean reps or load; every visit need not be harder.

sources.title: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults

quest.title: Spot a small step
quest.detail: In a made-up training log, mark the first clean rise in reps or load.

concepts.title: Muscle, protein and rest
concepts.hook: Training gives muscle a task. Food and time between hard sessions help the body respond.
concepts.rule: Resistance work is a growth signal. Protein in food gives building blocks, and rest gives time for change. One hard session alone does not do all the work.

claims.text: The ISSN stand gives about 1.4 to 2.0 grams of protein per kilogram per day for most exercising people.

items.stem: A hostel student trains with push-ups and eats dal, curd and meals across the day. What do the meals add?

options.text: Protein that helps build new muscle tissue.
options.feedback: Resistance work is a signal, while food brings the parts the body can use to respond.

options.text: The training signal, even if he skips resistance work.
options.feedback: Protein gives building blocks, so food can seem like the whole answer. Resistance work supplies a separate signal to adapt.

options.text: Instant muscle, however little he trains.
options.feedback: Food alone does not build muscle on the spot. Protein gives the parts, while training and time drive the change.

items.stem: At a college gym, Dev trains hard then has a normal canteen meal with dal and rice. What is the sound link?

options.text: Food protein can support the training response.
options.feedback: The stand says a varied daily diet can meet protein needs for active people.

options.text: Only a special product can make muscles adapt.
options.feedback: A shake can seem more direct. Normal food can give protein that helps the body respond to work.

options.text: The hard session alone, even with too little food.
options.feedback: The workout is vivid, so it can seem enough. Food gives parts for the response.

items.stem: For muscle training, about how many grams of daily protein per kilogram sit near the middle of the ISSN range for most active people?

options.text: About 1.7 grams per kilogram.
options.feedback: The stand gives a broad daily band from about 1.4 to 2.0 grams per kilogram.

options.text: About 0.8 grams per kilogram.
options.feedback: That lower goal may fit a less active person. The range here is for people who train.

options.text: About 4 grams per kilogram.
options.feedback: That is about twice the top of the ISSN range. The stand gives roughly 1.4 to 2.0 grams for active people.

items.stem: Which pair helps explain how resistance work can change muscle?

options.text: Training plus enough food and rest.
options.feedback: The exercise is the signal; food and time let the body respond to it.

options.text: A single hard set with no food.
options.feedback: The hard work stands out, so it can seem enough. Food and rest help the body respond.

options.text: Protein powder with no training at all.
options.feedback: Protein brings parts, but without the training signal there is little push for muscle to grow.

items.stem: A friend thinks adding protein to a meal can replace all resistance work for muscle growth. What part of the story is gone?

options.text: The training stimulus.
options.feedback: Protein supplies parts, while resistance work gives the muscle a reason to adapt.

options.text: The exact timing of a protein shake.
options.feedback: Shake timing can seem key. Yet food alone does not give muscles the work that helps them grow.

options.text: Enough rest by itself can replace the work.
options.feedback: Rest helps after training, so it can seem enough. It does not supply the first work signal.

items.stem: Fill the gap: resistance work is a signal; food protein brings ___.

options.text: Building blocks.
options.feedback: The body uses parts from food as it responds to the work done.

options.text: The whole training stimulus.
options.feedback: Food brings parts for growth, so it may seem like enough. Muscles also need the work signal.

options.text: Extra hours of sleep.
options.feedback: Sleep gives time to recover, but it comes from rest, not food. Protein in food brings building blocks.

items.stem: A classmate says the daily protein band is a target for every person, no matter what they do. What is the gap?

options.text: It is a range for most exercising people.
options.feedback: The stand ties that range to exercise, so it is not one rule for all people.

options.text: The stand gives one exact number for all people.
options.feedback: One number is easy to use. The stand gives a range for most people who train.

options.text: The top of the range is the target for every athlete.
options.feedback: A top value can look like a goal. Needs can vary within the range.

items.stem: Match each part of muscle growth to its job.

options.text: Resistance work
options.feedback: This work asks the muscle to do a hard task and can start change.

options.text: Signal to adapt
options.feedback: A training load gives the body a reason to grow more able.

options.text: Food protein
options.feedback: Meals bring protein that the body can use as it responds to work.

options.text: Parts for new tissue
options.feedback: The body can use parts from food as it builds after training.

misconceptions.name: One part is enough
misconceptions.correction: Training, food protein and time each play a part in muscle change.

quest.detail: In a made-up gym day, mark the work, the food and the time away from hard work.

concepts.title: Sleep and recovery
concepts.hook: A late exam night can make the next run feel harder and the canteen snack more tempting.
concepts.rule: Sleep helps the body and brain recover. Too little sleep can hurt exercise output and shift hunger. One short night does not give an exact result for every person.

claims.text: Adults are advised to get about 7 to 9 hours of sleep; sleep loss can harm exercise output and hunger cues.

items.stem: After a short hostel night, Ravi starts his usual run. What might he notice?

options.text: The run may feel harder.
options.feedback: Sleep loss can hurt exercise output, though no one night fixes the same result for all.

options.text: Only the workout can affect how his run feels.
options.feedback: It is tempting to judge a run only by its training plan. A short night can affect exercise output too.

options.text: He will run his best time yet.
options.feedback: A short night tends to lower exercise output, not lift it. A best time is less likely after poor sleep.

items.stem: During exams, a student sleeps less and feels more drawn to canteen snacks. Which link fits?

options.text: Sleep loss can shift hunger cues.
options.feedback: NIH notes that short sleep can change signals tied to hunger and fullness.

options.text: Sleep can have no link to appetite.
options.feedback: Hunger feels tied to meals, so sleep is easy to miss. A short night can shift those cues.

options.text: Exam stress alone explains it; sleep plays no part.
options.feedback: Stress may add to it, but short sleep itself can shift hunger and fullness signals, as NIH notes.

items.stem: For sleep that supports adult recovery, about how many hours a night sit near the middle of the NIH adult range?

options.text: About eight hours.
options.feedback: The NIH page gives seven to nine hours as the usual adult range.

options.text: About six hours.
options.feedback: Six hours can feel sufficient after a busy week, but it is below the cited adult sleep range.

options.text: About eleven hours.
options.feedback: Eleven hours sits above the usual adult range. NIH gives seven to nine hours for most adults.

items.stem: Which part of a training week gives the body time to recover?

options.text: Enough sleep and time away from hard work.
options.feedback: Sleep supports the body as it deals with the stress of exercise.

options.text: Only the hard sets themselves.
options.feedback: Training is the visible part. The body also needs time away from hard work to recover.

options.text: Extra sets on rest days.
options.feedback: More sets add more stress, not recovery. Sleep and time away from hard work let the body recover.

items.stem: A friend says one short night has no link to training because muscles only work during the session. What is missing?

options.text: Recovery and effort can change after sleep loss.
options.feedback: Sleep is part of the time when the body resets; less sleep can hurt later output.

options.text: A workout can end all need for recovery.
options.feedback: The session ends, so the work may seem done. The body still needs time to recover.

options.text: A short night matters only if the workout is skipped.
options.feedback: It is easy to count only missed sessions. Less sleep can also change how a run feels.

items.stem: Fill the gap: sleep helps keep hunger and fullness cues in ___.

options.text: Balance.
options.feedback: NIH says sleep helps the signals for feeling hungry or full work together.

options.text: One fixed pattern after each short night.
options.feedback: A short night can shift these cues, but it does not set the same response for all people.

options.text: Overdrive.
options.feedback: Good sleep does not push hunger up. NIH says it helps the hungry and full signals work together.

items.stem: A classmate reads that less sleep can hurt runs, then says every short night cuts each runner by the same amount. What is the gap?

options.text: A group trend is not one fixed personal result.
options.feedback: The review shows an average effect; people and tasks still differ.

options.text: Each runner gets an exact equal drop.
options.feedback: A study average is easy to reuse. Yet runners can respond in different ways.

options.text: The result must come from a single poor night.
options.feedback: One night may seem easy to blame. A group link does not pin down each person's cause.

items.stem: Which line best links sleep, training and appetite?

options.text: Sleep helps recovery and hunger cues.
options.feedback: Less sleep can change exercise output and the signals tied to food.

options.text: Sleep helps workouts but has no link to hunger cues.
options.feedback: Recovery gets the focus, so appetite is easy to miss. Sleep can shape both.

options.text: Sleep only matters before match days.
options.feedback: Sleep supports recovery and hunger cues every day, not just before a big game.

misconceptions.name: Sleep is separate from training
misconceptions.correction: Sleep can shape rest, sport and hunger cues.

concepts.title: Heat and hydration
concepts.hook: An Ahmedabad noon can make an outdoor session feel harder than the same work on a cool day.
concepts.rule: Heat adds strain and sweat takes fluid away. On hot days, a slower pace, breaks and water help reduce heat risk. Dizziness and nausea are warning signs to stop and cool down.

claims.text: Hot exercise can raise heat risk and fluid loss. Feeling dizzy, sick or headachy can be a warning.

items.stem: A hostel run moves from dawn to hot Ahmedabad noon. Which change fits the extra heat?

options.text: A slower pace with more breaks.
options.feedback: Heat adds strain, so easing the work and taking breaks can lower heat risk.

options.text: The same pace and breaks as on a cool morning.
options.feedback: A familiar route can feel like the same workout, but extra heat adds strain and calls for adjusting effort and breaks.

options.text: A faster pace, to finish before it gets hotter.
options.feedback: Rushing adds more heat strain. A slower pace with breaks lowers the risk on a hot day.

items.stem: At a college cricket game in heat, a player feels dizzy and sick. What do those signs call for?

options.text: Stop play and move to a cool place.
options.feedback: CDC lists these as heat signs and says to stop activity and cool down.

options.text: Drink water and keep playing at the same pace.
options.feedback: Water helps, so it can seem enough. Feeling dizzy or sick in heat calls for a stop.

options.text: Wait until the next break to cool off.
options.feedback: A planned break may feel close. These signs call for stopping now and moving to a cool place.

items.stem: During an hour of exercise in heat, about how much fluid can a person lose as sweat, according to CDC travel guidance?

options.text: About 1 litre.
options.feedback: CDC says sweat loss in heat may reach 1 litre per hour. Actual loss varies with conditions and effort.

options.text: About 100 millilitres.
options.feedback: A small drink may seem enough, but sweat loss in heat can be much larger: up to about 1 litre an hour.

options.text: About 10 litres.
options.feedback: Heat can increase fluid loss, but the CDC figure is about 1 litre per hour, not ten times that.

items.stem: Why does a hot-day session often need a lower pace?

options.text: Heat adds stress to the work.
options.feedback: The body has to shed heat while moving, so the same pace can be harder.

options.text: A trained runner can keep the same pace in any heat.
options.feedback: Fitness helps with a familiar workout, but heat adds strain even for trained people, so pace may need to fall.

options.text: Hot air makes muscles weaker for good.
options.feedback: Heat does not cause lasting weakness. The body is busy shedding heat, so the same pace feels harder for now.

items.stem: The Train hot-day mode cuts effort and adds breaks. Why does that make sense even for someone used to exercise?

options.text: Heat and sweat add a load beyond the workout.
options.feedback: Fitness does not remove heat strain; a lower pace and breaks can help.

options.text: Regular training stops all heat risk.
options.feedback: Being fit can feel like a shield. Hot weather still adds strain and fluid loss.

options.text: More sweat means the hard pace is safer to keep.
options.feedback: Sweat helps cool you, so this sounds right. It also means fluid is leaving the body.

items.stem: Fill the gap: when sweat takes fluid away, drinking water helps replace ___.

options.text: Some of that fluid.
options.feedback: Water can help cover the fluid that leaves the body as sweat.

options.text: All need for shade and breaks.
options.feedback: A drink can feel like a full fix. Heat still calls for shade and breaks.

options.text: Lost muscle.
options.feedback: Sweat takes away fluid, not muscle. Water helps cover some of that fluid loss.

items.stem: A teammate says dizziness is just proof that a hot run is working. What is the gap?

options.text: Dizziness can be a heat warning sign.
options.feedback: CDC lists it among signs to stop activity and get to a cool place.

options.text: Dizziness can show a safe effort target in heat.
options.feedback: Hard work can feel rough, which makes this tempting. In heat, feeling dizzy calls for a stop.

options.text: A drink is enough to keep the run going.
options.feedback: Water can help with fluid loss. It does not make a heat warning sign safe to ignore.

items.stem: Which line best sums up the hot-day mode in Train?

options.text: Less strain, more breaks and fluid.
options.feedback: The heat guide links hot activity with fluid loss and calls for a paced effort.

options.text: Keep the usual pace if you drink more water.
options.feedback: Water helps with fluid loss. It does not remove the heat load or warning signs.

options.text: Train hardest at noon to build heat strength.
options.feedback: Noon heat adds the most strain. Hot-day mode eases effort, adds breaks and keeps fluid up.

misconceptions.name: Heat is a bonus workout
misconceptions.correction: Heat adds strain and fluid loss; warning signs call for a stop and a cool place.

concepts.title: Warm-up and injury myths
concepts.hook: A few easy moves before hard work can let breathing and pulse rise bit by bit.
concepts.rule: A warm-up eases the start of hard work. Static holds can help range of motion, but long holds just before a power task may dull that next effort. No stretch makes injury risk vanish.

claims.text: A gradual warm-up raises heart rate and breathing; long static holds can slightly reduce later power in tests.

items.stem: Before hostel stair sprints, Neel walks and then jogs a little. What changes first?

options.text: Pulse and breathing rise in steps.
options.feedback: An easy start lets the heart and lungs build toward harder work.

options.text: Only his leg flexibility, not his pulse.
options.feedback: Warm-ups are often linked with stretching, but easy walking and jogging also raise the pulse gradually.

options.text: His muscles get longer for good.
options.feedback: An easy start does not change muscle length for good. It mainly lifts pulse and breathing step by step.

items.stem: At a college gym, a friend holds one long static stretch then tries a jump test. What may happen right after?

options.text: Jump output may dip a little.
options.feedback: The review found that longer holds can trim the next power test on average.

options.text: A long hold can boost every next jump.
options.feedback: More range can look like more power. A long hold may lower the next jump a little.

options.text: A long hold makes the next jump safer, whatever the task.
options.feedback: A stretch can feel like full prep. Its effect on risk can vary by task.

items.stem: For a warm-up before a sprint, a runner compares walking then jogging with a long still hold alone. About how many starts raise pulse in steps?

options.text: One: the walk then jog.
options.feedback: Walking then jogging raises effort in stages before the hard task.

options.text: Both starts do that job.
options.feedback: A still hold can change range of motion, but it does not raise pulse like easy movement.

options.text: None: only sprinting raises pulse.
options.feedback: Easy walking and jogging raise pulse too, just more gently. That is why the walk then jog counts.

items.stem: What is one job of an easy warm-up?

options.text: Let pulse and breath rise bit by bit.
options.feedback: The body moves from rest toward the harder task in a gradual way.

options.text: Hold one long stretch before any movement.
options.feedback: A static stretch can change range of motion, but an easy moving start gradually prepares the body for hard effort.

options.text: Tire the legs out before the main task.
options.feedback: A warm-up should ease the body in, not wear it out. Effort built in steps prepares it for harder work.

items.stem: A coach says a long static stretch always stops injury and gives the best next sprint. Which part needs care?

options.text: Neither result is certain for every task.
options.feedback: The review finds mixed injury data and a small power dip after long holds.

options.text: A long hold removes most injury risk.
options.feedback: A hold can feel like full prep. Its effect on injury risk is less clear.

options.text: A long hold must improve the next sprint.
options.feedback: More range may seem to mean more power. A long hold can lower power right after.

items.stem: Fill the gap: a static stretch means holding a pose rather than moving through it ___.

options.text: Again and again.
options.feedback: A still hold is the key part of static stretching, unlike a moving stretch.

options.text: Until the muscle feels fully warm.
options.feedback: A hold may feel warm, but static describes the held position rather than a required end point.

options.text: Only once a week.
options.feedback: Static is about holding still, not how often. The pose is held instead of moved through again and again.

items.stem: A classmate hears that long still holds can dull power and says all static stretching is bad. What is missing?

options.text: Static holds can also aid motion range.
options.feedback: The effect depends on task and dose; the review does not call every hold harmful.

options.text: Static holds harm every kind of movement.
options.feedback: A small power dip can stand out. A hold can still help range of motion.

options.text: Only a long hold can count as a warm-up.
options.feedback: A still stretch may feel like full prep. Easy motion can also raise pulse and breath.

items.stem: Which line best sums up a warm-up before hard play?

options.text: Build effort in steps and fit moves to the task.
options.feedback: A gradual start raises pulse and breath; stretch effects depend on the next task.

options.text: One long hold makes every task safe.
options.feedback: A stretch can feel like full prep. It cannot make every hard task safe.

options.text: Skip the start and go all out at once.
options.feedback: Jumping straight to full effort skips the build-up. A warm-up raises pulse and breath in steps first.

misconceptions.name: One stretch fixes all
misconceptions.correction: A warm-up can raise effort in steps; stretch effects vary by task and dose.

concepts.title: Cardio zones and talk test
concepts.hook: A walk can feel easy while a run makes speech come in short bursts. Breath gives a clue to effort.
concepts.rule: The talk test sorts effort by speech. At a moderate pace, talking works but singing does not. At a vigorous pace, only a few words fit before a breath. These are broad effort bands.

claims.text: CDC uses talk but not sing for moderate effort, and only a few words before a breath for vigorous effort.

items.stem: On a hostel walk, Mira can chat but cannot sing a line. Which effort band fits the talk test?

options.text: Moderate effort.
options.feedback: Being able to talk but not sing is the CDC clue for this broad band.

options.text: Vigorous effort, because singing is difficult.
options.feedback: Losing the ability to sing can sound like hard work, but being able to talk still fits the moderate band.

options.text: Rest, because she can still talk.
options.feedback: Being able to talk does not mean rest. Talking without singing is the CDC sign of moderate effort.

items.stem: During college cricket drills, Arjun can say only a few words before a breath. Which band is closer?

options.text: Vigorous effort.
options.feedback: Short speech bursts before a breath match the CDC clue for hard aerobic work.

options.text: Moderate effort, because he can still speak briefly.
options.feedback: A few words can sound like enough talk. This test puts such short speech in the hard band.

options.text: Easy effort, because cricket drills are short.
options.feedback: A short drill can feel easy to label. His brief speech points to hard effort.

items.stem: During cardio, a runner can talk but cannot sing. On CDC's 0-to-10 relative effort scale, about what rating fits this moderate band?

options.text: About 5 or 6 out of 10.
options.feedback: CDC links talking but not singing to moderate effort and rates that band about 5 or 6 out of 10.

options.text: About 2 out of 10.
options.feedback: Being able to speak may sound easy, but not being able to sing points to moderate effort, around 5 or 6.

options.text: About 9 out of 10.
options.feedback: At vigorous effort, speech usually shrinks to a few words before a breath. Talking freely points lower.

items.stem: What does the talk test use as a clue to effort?

options.text: How speech changes with breath.
options.feedback: As effort rises, talking and singing can become harder to keep up.

options.text: The speed shown on a watch.
options.feedback: Speed is easy to measure, but the same speed can feel different to different people; the talk test uses speech and breathing.

options.text: How sore the legs feel the next day.
options.feedback: Soreness comes later and varies a lot. The talk test reads effort in the moment from speech and breath.

items.stem: Two friends use the same bike speed; one can still sing and the other can only talk. Why can their effort bands differ?

options.text: The talk test tracks each person's felt effort.
options.feedback: The same outside pace can ask different amounts of work from different bodies.

options.text: A fixed speed gives all people the same effort.
options.feedback: Speed is easy to compare. Yet breath and fitness can make it feel quite different.

options.text: The one who can sing is working harder.
options.feedback: Singing can sound like extra work. In this test, easy singing points to a lower effort band.

items.stem: A runner can say full sentences but cannot sing. What changes first if the pace rises into the vigorous band?

options.text: Speech shrinks to a few words.
options.feedback: At a hard pace, a runner needs a breath after just a few words.

options.text: Singing becomes easy again.
options.feedback: Singing is hard at this pace. If effort rises, even speech gets short.

options.text: Talking gets easier and longer.
options.feedback: Harder effort leaves less breath for words. Speech gets shorter as the pace climbs into the vigorous band.

items.stem: A student says the talk test proves an exact heart-rate zone number for every runner. What is the gap?

options.text: It gives a broad effort clue.
options.feedback: Speech sorts rough bands; it does not read a pulse or set one number for all.

options.text: Speech gives an exact pulse count.
options.feedback: Breath and pulse both change with effort. Speech still cannot count each beat.

options.text: The same speech band gives one speed for all runners.
options.feedback: A common band can seem like a set pace. It is based on each runner's own breath.

items.stem: Which line best explains the talk test to a friend?

options.text: Speech gets shorter as aerobic effort rises.
options.feedback: Talking, singing and breath gaps offer a quick way to sort rough effort levels.

options.text: Speech stays the same at every pace.
options.feedback: A person can always try to talk. Hard effort can still cut words short.

options.text: If you can sing, you are working hard.
options.feedback: Singing with ease means light effort. As effort rises, singing goes first and then speech gets short.

misconceptions.name: One speed fits all
misconceptions.correction: The talk test gives broad effort bands that can differ between people.

sources.title: How to Measure Physical Activity Intensity
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

quest.title: Sort the talk clues
quest.detail: In a made-up walk, ride and run, mark where speech is easy, short or in between.

concepts.title: Habit of showing up
concepts.hook: A short hostel room session still counts as movement on a packed exam day.
concepts.rule: Some activity is better than none. Adults gain more with regular activity, and the WHO guide includes muscle work on two or more days each week. A short visit can keep a routine alive.

claims.text: WHO says some activity is better than none and advises adult muscle-strengthening work on two or more days a week.

items.stem: In a hostel exam week, Leena has time for a short bodyweight session, not her usual full one. Does it count as activity?

options.text: Yes, some movement still counts.
options.feedback: WHO says a short bout can help, even when it is less than the weekly goal.

options.text: Only a full session can count as activity.
options.feedback: The usual session feels like the standard. The guide counts even a short bout of work.

options.text: Only if it lasts at least an hour.
options.feedback: WHO sets no one-hour bar for movement to count. Even short bouts add up over the week.

items.stem: A college friend trains on two steady days and skips a rare all-out day. What fits the guideline better?

options.text: Regular muscle work on two days.
options.feedback: WHO lists two or more days for muscle work; regular visits make that possible.

options.text: One all-out day meets the two-day muscle goal.
options.feedback: A hard day feels like a lot. The guide counts days, so the second day still matters.

options.text: Muscle work only counts on weekends.
options.feedback: The guide counts days, not which days. Two or more days of muscle work in a week fits it.

items.stem: For an adult habit of muscle work, about how many days each week mark the WHO minimum in its activity guide?

options.text: Two days.
options.feedback: The guide sets two or more days of work for major muscle groups.

options.text: One all-out day each week.
options.feedback: One hard session can feel substantial, but the guide calls for muscle work on at least two days each week.

options.text: Six days.
options.feedback: That goes well past the minimum. The WHO guide asks for muscle work on two or more days.

items.stem: Which line fits the WHO guide when a person is just starting?

options.text: Some activity is better than none.
options.feedback: The guide says even a small amount of movement can have value.

options.text: Only the full target can have value.
options.feedback: A target looks like a pass mark. Some activity can help before that mark is reached.

options.text: Start with the hardest plan there is.
options.feedback: A very hard start is tough to repeat. The guide says some activity beats none, so small starts count.

items.stem: A student does one very hard gym day, then no activity for many weeks, and calls the whole term covered. What is missing?

options.text: The guide describes a weekly pattern.
options.feedback: One hard day does not fill the weeks that follow with muscle work.

options.text: One day keeps giving new work forever.
options.feedback: One hard day can feel like a lot. The guide still asks for a weekly pattern.

options.text: A very hard day can replace two steady days each week.
options.feedback: A hard burst can seem equal to more days. The muscle goal is set by days per week.

items.stem: Fill the gap: a brief walk can still be worth doing because some activity beats ___.

options.text: None.
options.feedback: WHO says a little movement has value even when it does not meet the full weekly aim.

options.text: A full workout target.
options.feedback: The full goal can seem like the bar. Yet a short walk still counts as some activity.

options.text: Rest days.
options.feedback: A good week includes rest. The WHO line compares a little movement with doing none at all.

items.stem: A friend says two muscle days are the whole activity guide, so walking has no place. What was left out?

options.text: The guide also includes aerobic movement.
options.feedback: It pairs muscle work with time spent in moderate or vigorous activity.

options.text: Only lifting matters for all health gains.
options.feedback: Two muscle days stand out in the guide. It also calls for aerobic work.

options.text: Walking counts only when it follows a gym day.
options.feedback: Gym days can feel like the main goal. A walk can count as activity on its own.

items.stem: Which line best sums up a workable training habit?

options.text: Start with some work and return to it.
options.feedback: Small bouts count. Coming back to weekly activity can help over time.

options.text: Wait until each day can be all-out.
options.feedback: A full plan can feel more useful. A short start still counts and is easier to repeat.

options.text: Train only on days you feel fully driven.
options.feedback: Drive comes and goes. Coming back for short sessions, even on flat days, builds the habit over time.

misconceptions.name: Only perfect sessions count
misconceptions.correction: A short session counts. Weekly work helps when it keeps coming back.

sources.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour
Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults

quest.detail: In a made-up week, mark the small sessions that keep activity present.

concepts.title: Food labels in India
concepts.hook: Two snack packs can show different serving sizes. The per 100 g line gives a common base to compare them.
concepts.rule: Indian labels can show a serving size and nutrients per 100 g. A common 100 g base makes sugar and protein easier to compare across packs. Total sugar and added sugar are different lines.

claims.text: FSSAI rules list a serve size. They also list protein and sugars for a set food amount, such as 100 g or one pack.

items.stem: At a hostel shop, two snack packs use different serving sizes. Which label line gives a fair same-amount comparison?

options.text: Nutrients per 100 g on both.
options.feedback: The same mass base lets sugar or protein be compared across the two packs.

options.text: Nutrients per different listed serve sizes.
options.feedback: The per-serve lines sit side by side. But the serves differ, so they lack one base.

options.text: Total nutrients per pack, even when pack sizes differ.
options.feedback: Pack totals seem easy to compare. Different pack sizes hide the nutrient amount per equal mass.

items.stem: A college student reads a canteen packet with 30 g per serve and 100 g per chart line. What does 30 g name?

options.text: The stated serve size.
options.feedback: The label names the amount used for one serve, which can differ by pack.

options.text: The fixed amount in every pack.
options.feedback: Thirty grams is printed, so it can look like a rule. Other packs may name another serve.

options.text: The protein in one serve.
options.feedback: Thirty grams is a weight of food, not a nutrient. It names the serve size the label uses.

items.stem: Two food labels use different serving sizes. For a fair sugar comparison, about how many grams should the common base contain?

options.text: 100 grams.
options.feedback: The per 100 g line puts both foods on the same mass, so serving-size differences do not distort the comparison.

options.text: Each pack's own serving size.
options.feedback: Each pack can define a different serve. A shared 100 g base lets the nutrient amounts be compared.

options.text: 1,000 grams.
options.feedback: A kilo is not the shared base on labels. The per 100 g line is the one used to compare packs.

items.stem: What does protein per 100 g tell a reader?

options.text: Protein in a set mass of that food.
options.feedback: The line gives the amount for one common mass, which helps compare packs.

options.text: Protein in any size of serving.
options.feedback: The label gives one clear number. That number is for 100 g, not every serve.

options.text: How much protein a body needs each day.
options.feedback: The line describes the food, not a person's needs. It gives the protein in 100 g of that food.

items.stem: One snack lists more protein per serving than another but also has a much larger serve. Why check the per 100 g lines?

options.text: They put both foods on one mass base.
options.feedback: A larger serve can raise the serve number even when the food has less protein per 100 g.

options.text: The larger serve must have denser protein.
options.feedback: More grams per serve can look richer. The serve may just be larger, so compare equal amounts.

options.text: The pack with more protein per serve always wins.
options.feedback: Per-serve totals are easy to compare. If serves differ, use the same mass first.

items.stem: Fill the gap: on an Indian nutrition label, total sugars and added sugars are ___ lines.

options.text: Different.
options.feedback: The label can show all sugars and the part added during food making.

options.text: Always the same.
options.feedback: Both lines say sugar, so they can look equal. Total can include sugar already in the food.

options.text: Optional.
options.feedback: Total and added sugars are two lines with different meanings. Total can include sugar already in the food.

items.stem: A student sees zero added sugar and says the total sugars line must also be zero. What is the gap?

options.text: Food may have sugars already in its parts.
options.feedback: Added sugar is one part of total sugar, so the two lines need not match.

options.text: Zero added sugar can erase all other sugars in a food.
options.feedback: Zero added can sound like zero total. Fruit or milk parts can still bring sugar.

options.text: The total sugars line counts only sugar added later.
options.feedback: The two lines sit close together, so they are easy to mix up. Total includes more.

items.stem: Which line best sums up a label check for sugar and protein?

options.text: Use the same 100 g base across packs.
options.feedback: Equal food amounts let the two nutrient lines mean the same kind of comparison.

options.text: Compare per-serve numbers even when serving sizes differ.
options.feedback: Per-serve figures are convenient, but unlike serving sizes can hide a difference; use a common amount and read both sugar lines.

options.text: Pick the pack with the bigger serve.
options.feedback: A bigger serve says nothing about sugar per gram. Both packs need the same 100 g base to compare.

misconceptions.name: Each serve is the same size
misconceptions.correction: Serving sizes can vary; per 100 g lines give a common food amount.

sources.title: Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020: compendium version VII
sources.publisher: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
